newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - July 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - July 7.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Federal Treasurer Peter Costello is aiming for a long-term economic cycle, rather than the short-cycles of the 1980s and 1990s, and is determined to see Australia's credit rating upgraded by restraining public spending before the next election. Costello said the Australian economy appears poised for a fall in unemployment, a long period of growth and higher levels of savings. Page 1.

In an effort to keep the Australian Labor Party solvent at the 1996 election, the national secretary Gary Gray deliberately misled then Prime Minister Paul Keating as to the amount of money spent on advertising during the federal election campaign. Gray told Keating the advertising budget had been increased as per the Prime Minister's demands, but he did not spend the money, convinced the ALP would lose the election. Page 1.

Market economists expect Australian Bureau of Statistics labour force data will show about 40,000 new jobs were created in June, when it is published on Thursday. This will show the Federal Government's target of 1.5 per cent employment growth for 1996-97 to be out of reach, and economists expect the unemployment rate to remain at just under nine per cent for most of this year. Page 3.

Even if management at Rio Tinto's Hunter Valley Number 1 mine succeed in breaking a picket and freight coal to the Newcastle port, a pact of solidarity between the Maritime Union of Australia and the Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union means waterfront bans would most likely stop the export of the coal. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Human rights groups fear the Howard Government's plan to remove a number of human rights commissioners will take away avenues for complaint and deny justice to minorities. Long-term plans for a new structure mean some specialist commissioners will be scrapped and complaints will be handled by general commissioners. Page 1.

The increase in federal meat inspection and registration fees has already affected Australia's meat exports, with cattle producers facing a price squeeze. A Northern Territory abattoir has closed and others have warned they will pass on higher costs to beef producers. Page 3.

Workers whose lives are potentially threatened every day suffer the highest amount of job-related stress, according to trauma counsellors. Police are the most affected, followed by ambulance officers, emergency room staff, rescue workers and the military.Page 3.

Lidcombe Children's Court heard yesterday that a 17-year-old boy threatened to blow up a Qantas plane on its way to Hong Kong, with his knowledge of explosives garnered from the Internet, if he was not paid more than A$500,000. The teenager was arrested on Saturday and charged. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The Holsworthy military range has become the favourite site for Sydney's A$5 billion second airport with some of Australia's leading politicians. Holsworthy is close to the Lucas Heights nuclear reactor and thousands of hectares of bush and deep river gorges must be bulldozed to build the airport on the site. Page 1.

It has been revealed that Federal Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser approached a local road design company in June last year, three months after taking over the portfolio, asking the company to consider slowing down traffic and beautifying parts of the street in which he lives. Page 3.

The Lidcombe Children's Court was yesterday told that a 17 year-old youth learnt about terrorist activities and bomb detonations from the Internet and threatened to blow up an airborne Qantas jet unless he was paid A$500,000. Police prosecutor Sergeant Dave Perry said the youth, who cannot be named because of his age, issued his demands when the jet, bound for Hong Kong, was in the air last Friday. Page 3.

The Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation, which led a consortium of four companies to conduct a feasibility study on the My Thuan bridge project in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, has admitted it did not inform the Federal Government it intended to bid for the A$83 million bridge contract and had "an interest" in seeing the project proceed. Page 2.
THE AGE

Foreign Minister Alexander Downer has confirmed that Australia is considering joining an international airlift to evacuate more than 500 Australian citizens trapped in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh by fierce fighting between forces loyal to Mr Hun Sen and his co-prime minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh. An airlift may use military transport aircraft via Thailand. Page A1.

Representatives at the Australian Uniting Church's highest policy-making council, the national assembly, have begun debating a report which recommends the ordination of practising gay or lesbian ministers. The report, Uniting Sexuality and Faith, also recommends forming a group to look at special marriage services to affirm committed homosexual relationships. Page A1.

Federal Coalition MP and monarchist Tony Abbott yesterday challenged the Australian Republican Movement to lobby the Senate to pass the Government's legislation for a constitutional convention on the republic. Republican Movement chairman Malcolm Turnbull refused to rule out the possibility of putting Opposition senators under pressure to pass the bill unamended. Page A3.

The Royal Australian Institute of Architects has condemned the selection project for the A$133 million National Museum in Canberra, advising its members that it could not endorse the design competition for the project. The Institute believes the selection process is being rushed, and that architects are being inadequately compensated for entering the competition. Page A3.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
